claims.evidence: This model is based on review articles synthesizing current understanding.

claims.claim: The current knowledge of ovule primordium growth in Arabidopsis is based on two-dimensional (2D) micrographs from tissue sections or clearing.
claims.source: Our current knowledge of ovule primordium growth in Arabidopsis is based on two-dimensional (2D) micrographs from tissue sections or clearing.
claims.evidence: This describes the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claims.claim: A 3D analysis of average cell volumes during primordium growth was recently provided.
claims.source: In addition, a 3D analysis of average cell volumes during primordium growth was recently provided (Lora et al., 2017), and extensive 3D analysis was carried on for late ovule stages (Vijayan et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This acknowledges recent related work in the field.

claims.claim: The reference collection comprises 92 segmented images with a total of 7763 annotated cells and five morphological cell descriptors.
claims.source: The collection of 92 segmented images, comprising a total of 7763 annotated cells and five morphological cell descriptors (volume, area, sphericity, prolate and oblate ellipticity), provides a unique resource for morphodynamic analyses of ovule primordium growth.
claims.evidence: This quantifies the data resource generated by the study.

claims.claim: The SMC appears morphologically distinct at late stages (2-I and 2-II) but not at early stages based on PCA analysis.
claims.source: In this global analysis, the SMC appears morphologically distinct at late stages (2-I and 2-II) but not at early stages.
claims.evidence: This finding is based on principal component analysis of cell descriptors shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claims.claim: Phase I (stages 0-I to 0-III) is characterized by a 4.5-fold increase in total cell number together with a moderate increase in mean cell volume (10%, p=0.03).
claims.source: Phase I (stages 0-I to 0-III) is characterized by a 4.5-fold increase in total cell number together with a moderate increase in mean cell volume (10%, p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This quantitative finding is based on analysis of segmented images with statistical significance.

claims.claim: Phase II (stages 1-I to 2-II) is characterized by a moderate increase in cell number (50%) and the global mean cell volume is relatively constant.
claims.source: By contrast, Phase II (stages 1-I to 2-II) is characterized by a moderate increase in cell number (50%) and the global mean cell volume is relatively constant (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Anisotropic organ growth during Phase I is confirmed by a steady increase in height, while primordium width increases moderately.
claims.source: Anisotropic organ growth during Phase I was confirmed by a steady increase in height, while primordium width increased moderately (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements of organ dimensions shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: In Phase I, a high proliferation activity was scored in L1 cells at the primordium apex (scoring 64% of all mitotic events).
claims.source: Consistent with our previous observation, in Phase I, a high proliferation activity was scored in L1 cells at the primordium apex (scoring 64% of all mitotic events).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of the CYCB1.1db-GFP mitotic reporter.

claims.claim: The L2 apical domain remains relatively quiescent during Phase I (only 3% of the mitotic events).
claims.source: By contrast, the L2 apical domain remains relatively quiescent (only 3% of the mitotic events).
claims.evidence: This is based on mitotic activity mapping using the CYCB1.1db-GFP reporter.

claims.claim: During Phase II, the majority (60%) of mitotic events is found in the basal domain.
claims.source: During Phase II, the majority (60%) of mitotic events is found in the basal domain, consistent with the progressive population of the basal domain with more cells.
claims.evidence: This finding is based on mitotic activity quantification shown in Figure 2H.

claims.claim: The distinct size of the SMC candidate is already detected at stage 0-III when compared to other L2,L3 cells.
claims.source: The distinct size of the SMC candidate is already detected at stage 0-III when compared to other L2,L3 cells (Figure 2I), or even earlier (stage 0-I) when compared to all other cells (Figure 2I inset).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through cell volume measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Cells from the L2 and L3 layers are larger than L1 cells already at stage 0-I.
claims.source: In addition, cells from the L2 and L3 layers are larger than L1 cells already at stage 0-I (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), possibly due to a longer growth phase, consistent with the low division frequency observed previously.
claims.evidence: This is based on cell volume comparisons shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: The SMC has a consistent anisotropic shape from early stages onwards, with a distinguishable major axis aligned with the primordium axis.
claims.source: This confirmed that the SMC has a consistent anisotropic shape from early stages onwards, with a distinguishable major axis aligned with the primordium axis.
claims.evidence: This is based on anisotropy analysis showing a mean angle of 22° (±11°, n = 16) between SMC major axis and ovule growth axis.

claims.claim: The Reference Model combines an initial, narrow domain of anisotropic, signal-based growth with a high concentration in inner layers, a broad domain competent for passive strain-based relaxation, and material anisotropy.
claims.source: This model combines the following hypotheses: an initial, narrow domain of anisotropic, signal-based growth with a high concentration in inner layers, a broad domain competent for passive strain-based relaxation, and material anisotropy (for FEM models only).
claims.evidence: This describes the parameters of the reference computational model.

claims.claim: Removing the growth anisotropy component abolished the digit shape of the primordium and produced a hemi-spherical protrusion in both FEM- and MS-based models.
claims.source: Removing the growth anisotropy component abolished the digit shape of the primordium and produced a hemi-spherical protrusion in both FEM- and MS-based models (Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—video 2).
claims.evidence: This demonstrates the necessity of growth anisotropy through model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: An inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth model, where the L1 also contributes to the expansion of the primordium, best described ovule primordium growth.
claims.source: Notably, an inner tissue-driven growth model, where the L1 also contributes to the expansion of the primordium, best described ovule primordium growth.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of different model scenarios.

claims.claim: Best-fit models produced by both cell- and tissue-based simulations predicted a growth-promoting signal in a confined domain along a vertical stripe at primordium emergence.
claims.source: In addition, best-fit models produced by both cell- and tissue-based simulations predicted a growth-promoting signal in a confined domain along a vertical stripe at primordium emergence.
claims.evidence: This prediction emerges from the modeling results.

claims.claim: In the Reference Model (MS-Model 2), an L2 apical cell with a trapezoidal shape, elongated along the main direction of ovule growth, emerged consistently during simulation.
claims.source: In the Reference Model (MS-Model 2), an L2 apical cell with a trapezoidal shape, elongated along the main direction of ovule growth, emerged consistently during simulation (note that these cells still divide in the models as no special rule has been assigned to them) (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This emergent property is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The elongated-trapezoidal shape of the SMC candidate emerges from the combination of assigned anisotropic cell growth and geometrical constraints imposed by the surrounding, growing tissues.
claims.source: The elongated-trapezoidal shape of such a cell is not a prescribed feature of the model, but rather emerges from the combination of assigned anisotropic cell growth and geometrical constraints imposed by the surrounding, growing tissues.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on analysis of the model behavior.

claims.claim: Katanin mutant primordia are 1.5 times bigger in volume than wild-type primordia (p=0.007, stage 0-III).
claims.source: kat mutant primordia clearly showed an increased size and a more isotropic shape (Figure 4A), being 1.5 times bigger in volume than wild-type primordia (p=0.007, stage 0-III, Figure 4B) with a smaller aspect ratio (p<0.01 stages 1-I, 1-II, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This quantitative difference is demonstrated with statistical significance in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Katanin mutant primordia have a smaller aspect ratio than wild-type (p<0.01 stages 1-I, 1-II).
claims.source: kat mutant primordia clearly showed an increased size and a more isotropic shape (Figure 4A), being 1.5 times bigger in volume than wild-type primordia (p=0.007, stage 0-III, Figure 4B) with a smaller aspect ratio (p<0.01 stages 1-I, 1-II, Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: At stage 0-III, kat ovules display a broader epidermis domain composed of more and larger cells than wild-type ovules (p=0.03 and p<0.001, respectively).
claims.source: Indeed, at stage 0-III, kat ovules display a broader epidermis domain composed of more and larger cells than wild-type ovules (p=0.03 and p<0.001, respectively) (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This finding is based on domain-specific cell quantification shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Mitosis frequency analysis in kat mutants indicated a shift in cell division from the apex toward the basis (2.4 times less mitoses in the L1 dome domain and 2.7 times more in the L1 basal domain, compared to the wild type).
claims.source: Mitosis frequency analysis indicated a shift in cell division from the apex toward the basis (2.4 times less mitoses in the L1 dome domain and 2.7 times more in the L1 basal domain, compared to the wild type) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), consistent with the increased cell number observed in L1.
claims.evidence: This is based on CYCB1.1db-GFP reporter analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: At stage 1-II, 34% of the kat primordia (n = 109) showed more than one enlarged, subepidermal cell; decreasing to 14% at stage 2-II (n = 104).
claims.source: At stage 1-II, 34% of the kat primordia (n = 109) showed more than one enlarged, subepidermal cell; decreasing to 14% at stage 2-II (n = 104), in stark contrast with wild-type primordia showing a majority (86% to 96%) of primordia with an unambiguous, single SMC (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This quantification is based on analysis of cleared ovule primordia shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: H1.1-GFP eviction occurred in more than one cell in 29% of kat primordia (n = 43).
claims.source: H1.1-GFP eviction occurred in more than one cell in 29% of kat primordia (n = 43, Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the H1.1-GFP marker shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: KNU-YFP was ectopically expressed in 21% of kat primordia at stage 1-II (n = 43).
claims.source: Detectable as early as stage 1-I in the wild type, it was ectopically expressed in 21% of kat primordia at stage 1-II (n = 43) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the KNU-YFP marker shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of AtDMC1-GUS was scored in 57% of kat primordia (n = 56).
claims.source: Third, to test whether the ectopic SMC candidates have a meiotic competence, we analyzed the AtDMC1-GUS reporter (Agashe et al., 2002; Klimyuk and Jones, 1997) and, indeed, scored ectopic expression in 57% of kat primordia (n = 56) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is based on GUS staining analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Using aniline blue staining, ectopic cells accumulating callose or ectopic tetrads were never detected in kat ovules (n = 119 and 269 ovules in bot1-7 and lue1, respectively).
claims.source: However, using aniline blue staining of callose deposition, which in wild-type SMCs stains the cell wall immediately before meiosis and marks the cells walls of tetrads after meiosis, we never detected ectopic cells accumulating callose or ectopic tetrads in kat ovules (n = 119 and 269 ovules in bot1-7 and lue1, respectively) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This negative result is based on callose staining analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: 21% kat primordia (n = 29) showed two cells labeled with pWOX2-CenH3-GFP marker at FG1 stage, as compared to 4% (n = 26) in the wild type.
claims.source: We next analyzed the pWOX2-CenH3-GFP marker labeling centromeres starting at the functional megaspore stage (FG1 stage) (De Storme et al., 2016) and found 21% kat primordia (n = 29) with two labeled cells, as compared to 4% (n = 26) in the wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the centromere marker shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: In the wild type, 27% of primordia (n = 289) had two SMC candidates (Class B) at stage 0-II, this frequency decreasing to 3% at stage 2-II (n = 103).
claims.source: In the wild type, the majority of ovules showed a single candidate SMC (Class A) at stage 0-II but 27% of primordia (n = 289) had two SMC candidates (Class B), this frequency decreasing to 3% at stage 2-II (n = 103).
claims.evidence: This quantification demonstrates the progressive restriction of SMC fate.

claims.claim: In wild-type primordia, SMC singleness is largely resolved at stage 1-I.
claims.source: Thus, instead of being immediate, SMC singleness can arise from a progressive restriction of fate among several SMC candidates during development. In wild-type primordia, SMC singleness is largely resolved at stage 1-I (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the developmental time course shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Plasticity in SMC emergence is higher in kat mutants with 42% (n = 202) class B primordia at stage 0-II compared to 26% (n = 289) in the wild type.
claims.source: Clearly, plasticity is higher with 42% (n = 202) class B primordia at stage 0-II in kat compared to 26% (n = 289) in the wild type.
claims.evidence: This comparison demonstrates increased plasticity in kat mutants.

claims.claim: The resolution process is delayed in kat mutants as up to 33% Class B primordia persist at stage 1-II (n = 113) compared to 12% in the wild type (n = 281).
claims.source: In addition, the resolution process is delayed in kat mutants as up to 33% Class B primordia persist at stage 1-II (n = 113) compared to 12% in the wild type (n = 281).
claims.evidence: This demonstrates delayed canalization in kat mutants.

claims.claim: Wild-type Class A and B primordia showed an enlarged nucleus in the candidate SMCs from stage 0-II onwards.
claims.source: Wild-type Class A and B primordia showed an enlarged nucleus in the candidate SMCs from stage 0-II onwards, and this correlation was also true in kat primordia (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
claims.evidence: This is based on nuclear area measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: In Phase I wild-type primordia, an S-phase pattern was captured in ~24% (n = 112) and ~40% (n = 79) of Class A primordia at stage 0-II and 0-III, respectively.
claims.source: This pattern was captured in a large proportion of primordia at stage 0-II and 0-III: ~24% (n = 112) and ~40% (n = 79) for Class A, respectively; 30% (n = 41) and 28% (n = 60) for Class B, respectively (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is based on PCNA-GFP reporter analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: In Phase II, SMC candidates showed no S-phase pattern in a large majority of both Class A and B primordia (97% on average, over entire Phase II).
claims.source: In Phase II, SMC candidates showed no S-phase pattern in a large majority of both Class A and B primordia (97% on average, over entire Phase II) (Figure 6G–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H) in agreement with the presence of newly replicated DNA at stage 1-I (She et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is based on PCNA-GFP analysis shown in Figure 6G-H and supported by cited literature.

claims.claim: In Phase II, kat primordia display a higher frequency of S-phase patterns in SMC candidates, suggesting that S-phase duration or entry is delayed compared to the wild type.
claims.source: Strikingly, in Phase II, kat primordia display a higher frequency of S-phase patterns in SMC candidates (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,H), suggesting that S-phase duration or entry is delayed compared to the wild type.
claims.evidence: This finding is based on PCNA-GFP analysis and represents an interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: The ovule primordium emerges from the placenta as a small dome-shaped protrusion and grows into a digit-shaped primordium with nearly cylindrical symmetry (stage 1-I) before enlarging at the base.
claims.source: The ovule primordium emerges from the placenta as a small dome-shaped protrusion and grows into a digit-shaped primordium with nearly cylindrical symmetry (stage 1-I) before enlarging at the base (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the morphological progression observed in the study.

claims.claim: The temporal resolution of the analysis led to subdivision of early stages (stage 0-I to stage 0-III) covering primordium emergence prior to the straight digit-shape of the organ set as stage 1-I.
claims.source: The temporal resolution of our analysis led us to subdivide early stages (stage 0-I to stage 0-III) covering primordium emergence prior to the straight digit-shape of the organ set as stage 1-I, where the SMC becomes distinguishable by its apparent larger size in longitudinal views (Grossniklaus and Schneitz, 1998; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This describes the refined staging system developed in this study.

claims.claim: Companion cells showed an increasing ellipticity (and decreasing sphericity), starting at stage 1-I and culminating at stage 2-I.
claims.source: Companion cells showed an increasing ellipticity (and decreasing sphericity), starting at stage 1-I and culminating at stage 2-I (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is based on shape analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The averaged maximum anisotropy shape index of the SMCs was consistently above the medium (and hence above the minimum) anisotropy index.
claims.source: The averaged maximum anisotropy shape index of the SMCs was consistently above the medium (and hence above the minimum) anisotropy index (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is based on anisotropy analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: The mean angle between SMC major axis and ovule growth axis at stage 0-II was 22° (±11°, n = 16).
claims.source: We measured the degree of alignment of the SMC major axis with the main growth axis of the ovule during early stages (stage 0-II) and found a mean angle of 22° (±11°, n = 16) (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: This quantitative measurement is shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: Two complementary 2D models of ovule primordium growth were developed: a finite element method (FEM)-based mechanical model and a mass spring (MS)-based model.
claims.source: For this, we developed two complementary 2D models of a longitudinal section of the ovule intersecting its main elongation axis: (i) a finite element method FEM-based mechanical model of the ovule represented as a continuous object (only outlining L1 vs. inner L2,L3 tissue) and (ii) a mass spring MS-based model of the ovule able to represent the mechanical status of each cell wall.
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling approaches used in the study.

claims.claim: Growth was implemented using two uncoupled but complementary modalities: signal-based growth and strain-based growth.
claims.source: Growth was implemented in both frameworks using two uncoupled but complementary modalities: (i) growth in which an abstract growth factor captures the cumulative effects of biochemical signals without considering their explicit mode of action (i.e. cell wall loosening, increasing turgor pressure), hereafter referred to as 'signal-based growth' (Boudon et al., 2015; Coen et al., 2004); and (ii) passive growth through relaxation of excess of strain inside the tissue, hereafter referred as 'strain-based growth' (Boudon et al., 2015; Bozorg et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling framework with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: When the growth signal is absent in the inner L2,L3 tissue, signal growth in the L1 alone is not sufficient to enable primordium growth.
claims.source: When the growth signal is absent in the inner L2,L3 tissue (FEM-Model 6, MS-Model 6), signal growth in the L1 alone is not sufficient to enable primordium growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Both models where a high level of growth signal is selectively present in L1 or in inner L2,L3 layers can produce a digit-shaped primordium.
claims.source: To conclude, both models where a high level of growth signal is selectively present in L1 or in inner L2,L3 layers can produce a digit-shaped primordium.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of different model scenarios.

claims.claim: Absence of a growth signal in the inner L2,L3 layers results in drastic shape alterations, favoring a scenario where inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth plays a fundamental role.
claims.source: Yet, absence of a growth signal in the inner L2,L3 layers results in drastic shape alterations. This favors a scenario where inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth plays a fundamental role.
claims.evidence: This interpretation is based on model results.

claims.claim: A broad tissue domain uniformly competent for strain accommodation is necessary to resolve the high accumulation of stress, which limits primordium elongation.
claims.source: Next, through modulation of passive strain-based growth, we determined that a broad tissue domain uniformly competent for strain accommodation is necessary to resolve the high accumulation of stress, which limits primordium elongation (FEM-Model 8, MS-Model 8, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Even in the case of isotropic material, it is possible to grow a digit-shaped protrusion, yet with a wider dome and increased L1 thickness, contrasting experimental observations.
claims.source: We also explored the contribution of material anisotropy for FEM-based simulations (FEM-Model 2 and FEM-Model 2a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C): even in the case of isotropic material, it is possible to grow a digit-shaped protrusion, yet with a wider dome and increased L1 thickness, contrasting experimental observations.
claims.evidence: This finding is based on FEM model simulations.

claims.claim: To restore L1 thickness in models with isotropic material, it is sufficient to prescribe material anisotropy exclusively in the L1.
claims.source: To restore L1 thickness, it is sufficient to prescribe material anisotropy exclusively in the L1 (FEM-Model 2a).
claims.evidence: This is based on FEM model simulations.

claims.claim: The SMC candidate does not display the stereotypical elongated, trapezoidal shape in MS-Model 3 with isotropic cell growth in inner layers.
claims.source: As Figure 3G–H shows, the SMC candidate does not display the stereotypical shape and is not even elongated.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations shown in Figure 3G-H.

claims.claim: Mild cell anisotropy can be reached in the SMC candidate if it is allowed to grow twice more than in the Reference Model.
claims.source: Yet, mild cell anisotropy can be reached if the SMC candidate is allowed to grow twice more than in the Reference Model (MS-Model 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in model simulations in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Directional cell growth in the epidermis is necessary to accommodate inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth and permit primordium elongation.
claims.source: The complementary model, altering cell growth anisotropy specifically in the L1, further suggested that directional cell growth in the epidermis is necessary to accommodate inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth and permit primordium elongation (MS-Model 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: When the SMC candidate was prevented from dividing in simulations, its enlargement overrode primordium shape control, creating an enlarged dome.
claims.source: When we prevented the SMC candidate to divide, its enlargement overrode primordium shape control in our simulations, creating an enlarged dome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: A mechanism may limit SMC growth in real ovule primordia to prevent overriding primordium shape control.
claims.source: This suggests that a mechanism may limit SMC growth in real ovule primordia.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the model behavior when SMC division is prevented.

claims.claim: In absence of the microtubule-severing protein KATANIN, the self-organization of cortical microtubules in parallel arrays is hindered, thereby decreasing the cellulose-dependent mechanical anisotropy of the cell wall, resulting in more isotropic growth.
claims.source: in absence of the microtubule-severing protein KATANIN, the self-organization of cortical microtubules in parallel arrays is hindered, thereby decreasing the cellulose-dependent mechanical anisotropy of the cell wall, resulting in more isotropic growth (Bichet et al., 2001; Burk and Ye, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about KATANIN function supported by cited literature.

claims.claim: KATANIN is expressed ubiquitously in the ovule, including both epidermal and internal L2,L3 tissue layers.
claims.source: Note that KAT is expressed ubiquitously and, thus, also in the ovule: the KATANIN protein could be detected in both epidermal and internal L2,L3 tissue layers using a GFP reporter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated using a GFP reporter shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Mutant primordia are clearly distinct from wild-type primordia in their relationship between aspect ratio and bounding box occupancy at stage 1-I.
claims.source: Mutant primordia are clearly distinct from wild-type primordia in their relationship between aspect ratio and bounding box occupancy at stage 1-I (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), when the primordium normally starts elongating along the major growth axis.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: These measurements confirmed a marked attenuation of anisotropic growth in kat ovule primordia as was observed in roots, shoot organs, or seeds.
claims.source: These measurements confirmed a marked attenuation of anisotropic growth in kat ovule primordia as was observed in roots, shoot organs, or seeds (Bichet et al., 2001; Hervieux et al., 2016; Luptovčiak et al., 2017b; Ren et al., 2017; Uyttewaal et al., 2012; Wightman et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This finding is consistent with prior observations in other tissues supported by cited literature.

claims.claim: At a global level, the mean cell number, cell volume, and sphericity are not significantly different between kat and wild-type primordia.
claims.source: Yet, at a global level, the mean cell number, cell volume, and sphericity are not significantly different between kat and wild-type primordia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is based on global quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: In kat SMC neighbors at stage 0-II, there is an increased relative frequency of CYCB1.1db-GFP expression, whereas it decreases at stage 1-II.
claims.source: When specifically looking at the L2 apical domain, where the SMC differentiates, we noticed an increased relative frequency of CYCB1.1db-GFP expression in kat SMC neighbors at stage 0-II, whereas it decreases at stage 1-II (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on mitotic reporter analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: This is in stark contrast with SMC neighbors in wild-type primordia displaying first a relative mitotic quiescence at stage 0-II, and then enhanced mitotic activity at stage 1-II.
claims.source: This is in stark contrast with SMC neighbors in wild-type primordia displaying first a relative mitotic quiescence at stage 0-II, and then enhanced mitotic activity at stage 1-II.
claims.evidence: This comparison highlights the altered temporal pattern in kat mutants.

claims.claim: In the SMC, no mitotic activity increase was observed in kat as compared to wild-type primordia.
claims.source: Yet, in the SMC, no mitotic activity increase was observed in kat as compared to wild-type primordia (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on mitotic reporter analysis.

claims.claim: The most parsimonious hypothesis is that the altered geometry in kat primordia expands the domain of cells competent to form SMCs.
claims.source: The most parsimonious hypothesis is that the altered geometry in kat primordia expands the domain of cells competent to form SMCs.
claims.evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the kat phenotype.

claims.claim: Isotropic cell growth and altered mechanical constraints in the tissue acting from primordia emergence onwards lead to divisions and patterning alterations that expand the domain of cells competent for SMC fate.
claims.source: In this scenario, isotropic cell growth and altered mechanical constraints in the tissue acting from primordia emergence onwards, lead to divisions and patterning alterations that expand the domain of cells competent for SMC fate.
claims.evidence: This is the proposed working model based on the data.

claims.claim: SMC candidates emerge from within a mitotically quiescent L2 apical domain.
claims.source: We found that SMC candidates emerge from within a mitotically quiescent L2 apical domain, consistent with the finding that the H3.1 histone variant HTR13 is evicted, marking cell cycle exit (Hernandez-Lagana and Autran, 2020).
claims.evidence: This finding is consistent with cited work on histone variant eviction.

claims.claim: SMC candidates have a markedly long S-phase compared to surrounding cells.
claims.source: In addition, SMC candidates have a markedly long S-phase compared to surrounding cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on PCNA-GFP reporter analysis.

claims.claim: These observations are reminiscent of the animal germline where mitotic quiescence is a prerequisite for meiosis.
claims.source: These observations are reminiscent of the animal germline where mitotic quiescence is a prerequisite for meiosis (Kimble, 2011; Reik and Surani, 2015).
claims.evidence: This comparison to animal systems is supported by cited literature.

claims.claim: Early SMC candidates already display a typically large cell and nucleus size and an elongated shape aligned with the primordium growth axis.
claims.source: Also, early SMC candidates already display a typically large cell and nucleus size and an elongated shape aligned with the primordium growth axis.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of cell and nuclear characteristics.

claims.claim: SMC characteristics are established much earlier than previously thought, that is, soon after primordium emergence (stages 0-II/0-III).
claims.source: Collectively, we found that SMC characteristics are established much earlier than previously thought, that is, soon after primordium emergence (stages 0-II/0 III).
claims.evidence: This is a key finding that revises previous understanding.

claims.claim: These characteristics frequently arise in more than one SMC candidate at Phase I, typically resolving into a single SMC at the onset of Phase II.
claims.source: Moreover, these characteristics frequently arise in more than one SMC candidate at Phase I, typically resolving into a single SMC at the onset of Phase II.
claims.evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of SMC fate restriction.

claims.claim: This clearly documents a developmental sequence of plasticity at SMC fate emergence and progressive resolution of SMC fate to a single cell.

claims.source: SMC fate emergence is characterized by mitotic quiescence and cellular growth in one or more L2 apical cells.

results.result: The authors generated a comprehensive 3D image dataset of 92 annotated ovule primordia at cellular resolution, comprising 7763 cells with five morphological descriptors, and developed a refined staging system subdividing early developmental stages (0-I to 0-III) prior to the digit-shaped stage 1-I.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C17, and C53 collectively describe the creation of a well-documented image resource with explicit numbers of images, cells, and descriptors. The staging refinement is clearly justified and documented in Table 1 and Figure 1. This represents a solid methodological foundation for the study.

results.result: Ovule primordium development occurs in two distinct phases: Phase I (stages 0-I to 0-III) characterized by 4.5-fold increase in cell number with high proliferation in L1 apical cells (64% of mitotic events), and Phase II (stages 1-I to 2-II) with moderate cell number increase and mitotic activity shifted to the basal domain (60% of events).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 provide quantitative evidence from both segmented images and CYCB1.1db-GFP reporter analysis showing biphasic, domain-specific cell division patterns. Statistical significance is reported (p=0.03 for Phase I volume increase), and the findings are internally consistent across multiple measurement approaches. Claim C2 accurately summarizes this spatio-temporal pattern.

results.result: SMC characteristics emerge much earlier than previously recognized (stages 0-II/0-III), with candidate SMCs displaying distinct size, enlarged nuclei, and anisotropic shape aligned with the primordium axis (mean angle 22° ± 11°) from early developmental stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27, C84-C85 are supported by quantitative measurements of cell volume, nuclear area, and anisotropy indices shown in Figures 2I-K and 6D. The early emergence finding revises previous understanding and is well-documented with statistical comparisons. The 22° alignment angle provides specific quantitative support.

results.result: Computational modeling using both FEM and MS approaches identified plausible morphogenetic principles: inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth with a spatially confined growth signal, passive strain-based relaxation in a broad domain, and anisotropic cell growth are necessary for digit-shaped primordium formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 describe modeling results that converge across two independent computational approaches (FEM and MS). The necessity of growth anisotropy is demonstrated by ablation experiments (C29), and the role of inner tissue growth is shown through systematic parameter variation. Claim C3 accurately summarizes these findings. The convergence of two modeling frameworks strengthens confidence.

results.result: The elongated-trapezoidal SMC shape emerges as a property of tissue geometry and mechanical constraints in the reference model, but requires anisotropic cell growth specification; isotropic growth models fail to produce the stereotypical SMC shape unless the SMC is allowed to grow twice as much.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 and C66-C67 demonstrate through MS-Model simulations that SMC shape is an emergent property dependent on growth anisotropy. The comparison between reference and variant models (MS-Model 2 vs MS-Model 3) provides clear evidence. However, the interpretation relies on 2D simulations which may not fully capture 3D complexity.

results.result: Katanin mutant primordia show altered geometry with 1.5-fold increased volume (p=0.007), smaller aspect ratio (p<0.01), broader epidermis with more and larger cells (p=0.03 and p<0.001), and shifted mitotic activity from apex to base, confirming attenuated anisotropic growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37, C73-C74 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of kat phenotype with appropriate statistical tests and multiple independent measurements. The findings are consistent with prior observations in other tissues (C74 with citations). Sample sizes are adequate (n=59 annotated 3D images for kat dataset).

results.result: Katanin mutants show ectopic SMC candidates with molecular markers of SMC identity: 34% show multiple enlarged cells at stage 1-II, 29% show H1.1-GFP eviction in multiple cells, 21% show ectopic KNU-YFP expression, and 57% show ectopic AtDMC1-GUS expression, but no ectopic callose deposition or tetrads were detected.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 provide convergent evidence from multiple independent markers (morphology, H1.1-GFP, KNU-YFP, AtDMC1-GUS, callose, pWOX2-CenH3-GFP) with adequate sample sizes. The negative result for callose (C42) is important and well-documented (n=119 and 269 ovules). The findings suggest ectopic SMC candidates acquire some but not all SMC characteristics.

results.result: SMC fate undergoes progressive canalization: in wild-type, 27% of primordia show two SMC candidates at stage 0-II, decreasing to 3% at stage 2-II (resolved by stage 1-I); in kat mutants, plasticity is increased (42% at stage 0-II) and resolution is delayed (33% persist at stage 1-II vs 12% in wild-type).
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are based on analysis of 1276 wild-type and 2587 kat primordia across multiple alleles, providing robust statistical power. The progressive restriction is well-documented and the delay in kat mutants (C6, C47) provides experimental support for the role of geometry in fate restriction. Claims C4-C5 accurately summarize these findings.

results.result: SMC candidates display distinct cell cycle patterns: in Phase I, S-phase is detected in ~24-40% of wild-type primordia suggesting a markedly long S-phase; in Phase II, 97% of SMC candidates show no S-phase pattern, while kat mutants show higher S-phase frequency suggesting delayed S-phase entry or duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51, C82 are based on PCNA-GFP reporter analysis with adequate sample sizes (n=112-79 for Phase I). The interpretation of long S-phase (C82) is reasonable given low mitotic frequency. The kat phenotype (C51) provides additional support. However, the marker cannot definitively distinguish meiotic from mitotic S-phase.

results.result: The study proposes that tissue geometry channels reproductive cell fate in the ovule primordium: altered geometry in kat mutants expands the domain of cells competent for SMC fate through isotropic cell growth and altered mechanical constraints, similar to geometry-dependent canalization in animal systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C79-C80, C97-C99 represent the main conceptual conclusion integrating modeling predictions with kat phenotype. The parsimonious hypothesis (C79) is well-supported by the convergence of computational predictions and experimental observations. The parallel to animal systems (C97) is appropriately cited. However, this remains a proposed mechanism requiring additional experimental validation.

results.result: SMC fate emergence is characterized by mitotic quiescence in the L2 apical domain, enlarged nuclei in candidate SMCs from stage 0-II onwards, and cellular growth; resolution involves re-entry into somatic cell cycle and re-incorporation of H3.1 histone in neighboring cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C81, C95-C96 describe cellular events during SMC specification supported by nuclear area measurements (Figure 6D), mitotic reporter analysis, and cited work on H3.1 eviction (Hernandez-Lagana and Autran, 2020). The findings are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Model simulations reveal that signal growth in L1 alone is insufficient for primordium growth when absent in inner L2,L3 tissue; inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth plays a fundamental role; broad strain accommodation is necessary; and directional epidermal growth is required to accommodate inner tissue growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63, C68 describe systematic parameter variations in both FEM and MS models (Models 5-8) showing the necessity of different growth components. The conclusions are based on comparison of multiple model scenarios with clear phenotypic outcomes. The convergence across modeling approaches strengthens the findings.

results.result: FEM simulations show that isotropic material can produce digit-shaped protrusions but with wider dome and increased L1 thickness; material anisotropy exclusively in L1 is sufficient to restore L1 thickness control.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 describe FEM-specific findings (Models 2 and 2a) about material properties. The results are clearly shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and provide insights into L1 thickness control. However, MS models cannot test material anisotropy, limiting cross-validation.

results.result: When SMC division is prevented in simulations, its enlargement overrides primordium shape control creating an enlarged dome, suggesting a mechanism may limit SMC growth in real primordia.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 describes a simulation result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G. However, claim C70 is speculative inference about a compensatory mechanism (possibly turgor pressure reduction) that lacks experimental validation. The simulation result is clear but the biological interpretation requires further investigation.

results.result: Quantitative shape analysis reveals that SMC appears morphologically distinct at late stages (2-I, 2-II) but not early stages by PCA; companion cells show increasing ellipticity from stage 1-I; SMC displays consistent anisotropy with maximum index above medium/minimum indices.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C55-C57 describe shape quantification results from PCA and anisotropy analysis. The findings are based on the comprehensive dataset with appropriate computational methods (MorphoMechanX extension). The 22° alignment angle (C57) provides specific quantitative support.

results.result: KATANIN is expressed ubiquitously in ovule including L1 and L2,L3 layers; global cell parameters are not significantly different between kat and wild-type, but domain-specific analysis reveals altered mitotic patterns in L2 apical SMC neighbors (increased at stage 0-II, decreased at stage 1-II) contrasting with wild-type pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C75-C78 provide important context for interpreting kat phenotype. KATANIN localization (C72) is demonstrated with GFP reporter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The domain-specific mitotic alterations (C76-C78) are based on CYCB1.1db-GFP analysis and explain the ectopic SMC phenotype.

results.result: Two complementary 2D modeling approaches were developed: FEM-based continuous tissue model and MS-based cell wall network model, both implementing signal-based and strain-based growth modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 describe the modeling methodology with appropriate citations to prior work (Boudon et al., 2015; Coen et al., 2004; Bozorg et al., 2016). The dual approach allows cross-validation and testing of different hypotheses. Methods are described in detail in Appendix 1.

results.result: The study documents developmental canalization at the cellular domain level in ovule primordium, where L2 apical cells initially share SMC competence leading to plasticity, followed by progressive fate restriction to a single SMC; this process remains robust despite genetic perturbations and is consistent with prior hypotheses.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87, C91-C94 describe the canalization framework supported by quantitative data on SMC candidate frequencies across development. The connection to prior hypotheses (C93) and robustness despite mutations (C94) are well-supported. Claim C91 about expanding examples of canalization is justified.

results.result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about germline specification in plants vs animals, SMC characteristics, natural variation in SMC singleness, regulatory pathways controlling SMC fate, and prior 2D/3D imaging approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C16 represent established knowledge and prior work appropriately cited from the literature. These provide necessary context for the study. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are standard for the field.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within established knowledge: KATANIN function in cell wall anisotropy, parallels to animal germline quiescence, and the concept of developmental canalization in both animal and plant systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C83, C88-C90 represent established knowledge appropriately cited to provide context for interpreting the study's findings. The citations to canalization literature (Waddington, 1942; Hallgrimsson et al., 2019) and animal/plant examples are appropriate.

results.result: The image resource is complementary to existing datasets capturing later ovule stages and contributes to building a developmental atlas integrating morphogenesis with gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 appropriately position the resource in the context of related work (Lora et al., 2017; Vijayan et al., 2021; Wolny et al., 2020; Hartmann et al., 2020). The dataset is publicly available at DRYAD repository as stated in methods.
